### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Whence has it all the materials of reason and knowledge? To this I answer, in one word, from experience.”

English

“Whence has it all the materials of reason and knowledge? To this I answer, in one word, from experience.”

Seventeenth-century English, capitalised as Locke wrote it. The question is his own, put in order to be answered.

### Attribution notes

An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, II.i.2. The doctrine is routinely labelled “tabula rasa,” and that Latin phrase is not Locke's — it comes from earlier scholastic and Aristotelian usage. Locke's own image in the same chapter is “white paper.” The substitution matters because “blank slate” suggests an entirely passive mind, whereas the chapter's point is about the origin of ideas, not about the absence of innate powers.

#### About John Locke

John Locke (1632–1704) was the English philosopher of empiricism and liberal politics whose Essay Concerning Human Understanding and Two Treatises of Government defined a century’s agenda. Associated with Shaftesbury and the Glorious Revolution settlement, he wrote on toleration, education, and money.

### How to read this passage

Empiricists treat experience as the source of ideas; phenomenologists describe its structure; pragmatists treat it as experimental and revisable. This passage enters that discussion through experience, knowledge.
